READING 40
EQUITY JURISDICTIONS, CLASSES,
AND THE VOTING PROCESS
MODULE 40.1: RIGHTS OF EQUITY
SHAREHOLDERS
LOS 40.a: Describe differences in economic and voting rights and other
characteristics among different jurisdictions and equity classes.
In our previous reading, we described the economic and voting rights of equity
shareholders. These rights may vary if a company has different classes of shares
or if an investor owns shares in a foreign company.
Foreign Shares
Many investors exhibit home asset bias, overweighting their portfolios with
assets in their home countries. One way to counteract home asset bias in a
portfolio is by investing in foreign shares.
Direct investing in the securities of foreign companies refers to buying a foreign
firm’s securities in foreign markets. Some of the obstacles to direct foreign
investment include the following:
Investors incur extra costs to set up securities accounts in foreign markets.
Investors must be familiar with the procedures of each market in which they
invest, such as the clearing and settlement of trades.
Taxation rules are likely to be different in a foreign market than in an investor’s
home market.
Trading hours may be different than an investor’s home market.
Reporting requirements of foreign stock exchanges may be different, and
required disclosures may be in an unfamiliar foreign language.

The investment and return are denominated in a foreign currency, which adds
foreign exchange risk and additional transactions costs to an investment.
Some countries might regulate or tax the return of capital to an investor’s home
country.
A foreign stock exchange may be illiquid.
Investors can also gain exposure to foreign shares through indirect investing
vehicles that mitigate some of the obstacles to direct investing. One such method
is a depository receipt (DR). DRs represent ownership in a foreign firm and are
traded in the markets of other countries in local market currencies.
To create a DR, a domestic bank holds shares deposited by the foreign firm and
then issues receipts representing ownership of a specific number of the foreign
shares. This depository bank acts as a custodian and manages dividends, stock
splits, and other events. Although the investor does not have to convert to the
foreign currency, the value of a DR is affected by exchange rate changes,
alongside factors that affect the value of any stock such as firm fundamentals
and economic events. To prevent arbitrage, the price of a DR should equate to
the foreign share price at the current exchange rate, but in some situations the
arbitrage relationship breaks down.
DRs are often referred to by the markets where they are listed. For example,
American depository receipts (ADRs) are denominated in US dollars and trade
in the United States, and European depository receipts (EDRs) trade in Europe
and are typically denominated in euros.
Global depository receipts (GDRs) are issued outside the United States and
outside the issuer’s home country. Although not listed on US exchanges, they are
usually denominated in US dollars and can be sold to US institutional investors.
GDRs are not subject to the capital flow restrictions imposed by governments, so
they offer the firm and the investor greater opportunities for foreign investment.
The firm usually chooses to list the GDR in a market where many investors are
familiar with the firm.
If the firm is involved with the issue, a DR is a sponsored DR; otherwise, it is
an unsponsored DR. A sponsored DR provides the investor voting rights and is
usually subject to greater disclosure requirements. In an unsponsored DR, the
depository bank retains the voting rights.

Some large multinational firms encourage share ownership by nondomestic
investors through dual listing, in which their shares trade on one or more foreign
stock exchanges in addition to an exchange in their home market.
Dual-Class Share Structures
A firm may have different classes of common stock (e.g., Class A and Class B
shares). Such a dual-class share structure often involves some classes of
common stock having greater voting rights than others. This can give a specific
group of shareholders, such as a company’s founders, effective control of the
company while holding less than a majority of shares.
Share classes may also be treated differently with respect to economic rights,
such as dividends. In some cases, economic rights of different share classes may
be in the same proportions as their voting rights. In other cases, one class of
common shares may have greater economic rights, while another class has
greater voting rights.
Information on the economic and voting rights of different classes of equity
shares can be found in the company’s filings with securities regulators, such as
the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in the United States.
LOS 40.b: Describe the voting process and roles of the issuer’s
management, board, proxy advisors, asset managers, and asset owners in
the process.
As we saw in our Corporate Finance reading on corporate governance, voting
rights are how share owners can exercise their authority over a company’s
actions.
Many of the matters that shareholders vote on routinely, such as the selection of
an auditor or candidates for the board of directors, are put forth by a company’s
management or board. However, share owners themselves can also introduce
shareholder proposals for actions they believe a company should take.
Shareholder proposals are typically nonbinding, but if they attract significant
support, they can signal management about issues the shareholders expect them
to address. While a company does not have to present all shareholder proposals
for a vote, financial market regulations may require management to provide
reasons for rejecting one.

Share voting occurs at a company’s annual meeting. Shareholders may attend the
meeting or vote by proxy, typically with a slightly earlier cutoff date than that for
shareholders who attend the meeting.
The company determines which matters need to be presented to shareholders and
solicits shareholder proposals. This needs to occur far enough ahead of the
annual meeting to allow the company to prepare a proxy statement for the
annual meeting, which provides the meeting agenda, lists all proposals to be
voted on (often with management’s or the board’s recommendations on voting
for or against the proposals), and discloses the requirements and deadlines for
voting.
In most cases, equity shares are held by a custodian broker or bank in the name
of the shares’ beneficial owner. One of the custodian’s responsibilities is
distributing proxy statements to shareholders. Another is determining the
shareholder of record who is eligible to vote at the annual meeting. The record
date for voting eligibility is often 30 days or more ahead of the meeting. A
shareholder who sells the stock after the record date but before the meeting
remains eligible to vote the shares.
Investors may choose to delegate their proxy votes to asset managers. As we will
see in the Ethical and Professional Standards topic area, asset managers who are
CFA Institute members or candidates are required to vote proxies on relevant
issues in an informed and responsible manner and should vote in the interests of
the shares’ beneficial owners, per Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care.
Institutional investors such as mutual funds routinely hold equity shares in many
different companies across multiple markets. To exercise their voting rights
responsibly, institutional investors often rely on proxy advisors, firms that
specialize in recommending how to vote proxies based on the most current
information and in line with principles of corporate governance.
MODULE QUIZ 40.1
1. Global depository receipts (GDRs) are most often denominated in:
A. US dollars and issued in the United States.
B. US dollars and issued outside the United States.
C. the currency of the country where they trade and issued outside the United States.
2. A company has various securities outstanding. Which of the following most likely
indicates that the company has a dual-class share structure?
A. Common shareholders may vote on company matters, but preferred shareholders may
not vote.

B. Some of a company’s bonds are convertible to common shares, while some of its
bonds are not convertible.
C. Some common shares give the holder two votes on company matters, while other
common shares give the holder one vote.
3. An investor hears about a shareholder proposal at XYZ Company that will be voted on at
the company’s annual meeting the following week. The investor buys 100 shares of XYZ,
and the trade settles two days before the meeting. Can this investor vote on the
shareholder proposal?
A. No.
B. Yes, because the shareholder is the beneficial owner.
C. Yes, because the investor is the shareholder of record.
KEY CONCEPTS
LOS 40.a
Direct investing in the securities of foreign companies refers to buying a foreign
firm’s securities in foreign markets. Direct investing involves foreign exchange
risk and costs of setting up and monitoring investments in markets that may be
unfamiliar to the investor.
Depository receipts (DRs) that trade in local market currencies are vehicles for
indirect investment in foreign companies. Although the investor does not have to
convert to the foreign currency, the value of a DR is affected by exchange rate
changes.
A dual-class share structure involves some classes of common stock having
greater voting rights or economic rights than others. This structure can give
effective control of a company to a specific group of shareholders, such as its
founders.
LOS 40.b
A company’s management and board of directors propose routine matters for
shareholder votes. Shareholders may also make their own proposals, which are
typically nonbinding on management but can signal issues that shareholders
expect management to address.
Share voting occurs at a company’s annual meeting. A proxy statement provides
the meeting agenda, lists proposals to be voted on, and discloses the
requirements and deadlines for voting.

If shares are held by a custodian, the custodian is responsible for determining the
shareholder of record for proxy votes. The record date for eligibility is often 30
days or more ahead of the annual meeting.
Investors can vote proxies themselves or delegate their votes to asset managers.
Proxy advisors are firms that assist institutional investors in managing their
proxy votes.
ANSWER KEY FOR MODULE QUIZ
Module Quiz 40.1
. B GDRs are not listed on US exchanges and are most often denominated in
US dollars. They are not issued in the United States. (LOS 40.a)
. C A dual-class share structure refers to common shares that have different
economic or voting rights. (LOS 40.a)
. A The record date for proxy voting is typically 30 days or more before the
company’s annual meeting, to allow time for preparing and distributing the
proxy statement. (LOS 40.b)
